rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)}} + \mathrm{Ag_2O_{(s)}} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}_{(aq)}} + 2\mathrm{Ag_{(s)}} + 2\mathrm{OH^{-}_{(aq)}}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = 0.80\) V
\(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\) V
1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
\(\Delta_r \mathrm{G^{o}}\) for the above reaction is :
rows.solution:
The reaction takes zinc to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) and silver from \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\) down to metallic silver, so zinc is oxidised at the anode and silver reduced at the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56\ \mathrm{V}\)
Two electrons are transferred, as the balanced equation shows, so \(n = 2\) and
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.56 = -301080\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
which is \(-301.080\) kJ \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). The sign matters as much as the size: a spontaneous cell reaction must give a negative free energy change, which rules out the positive value offered among the choices.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Identify the correct statement :

options.label: A
options.text: Molecularity of a reaction is an experimental quantity.

options.label: B
options.text: For complex reactions molecularity has no meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: Molecularity of a reaction can be zero or even a fraction.

options.label: D
options.text: Molecularity more than three is very common in chemical reactions.

rows.solution: Molecularity is the number of species that must collide simultaneously for an elementary reaction to occur, so it is defined by the mechanism and not measured. That immediately fixes the four statements. It is a theoretical quantity, not an experimental one — order is the experimental quantity. It must be a whole number counting colliding particles, so it can be neither zero nor a fraction. A simultaneous collision of more than three particles is so improbable that molecularity above three is essentially never seen. And a complex reaction proceeds through several elementary steps, each with its own molecularity, so the reaction as a whole has none: that is the statement which is correct.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The order for the given reaction is :
\(\mathrm{A} + 2\mathrm{B} \rightarrow\) Products
Rate \(= \mathrm{k[A]}^{1/2}\,\mathrm{[B]}^{1}\)
rows.solution:
The order of a reaction is the sum of the exponents on the concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law — not the sum of the stoichiometric coefficients, which here would wrongly give 3. From
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{1/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{1}\)
the exponents are \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(1\), so the order is \(\tfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 1.5\).

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem: Electronic configuration of chromium is :
rows.solution: Chromium has 24 electrons, and filling the orbitals in the ordinary way would give \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^4 4s^2\). It does not. The \(3d\) and \(4s\) levels are very close in energy, so promoting one \(4s\) electron into \(3d\) costs little and buys the extra stability of two exactly half-filled subshells. The ground state configuration is therefore \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\). Copper does the same thing one step further along, reaching \(3d^{10} 4s^1\).

rows.stem: The correct IUPAC name of the complex \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) is :
rows.solution: The complex is neutral overall. Ligands are named in alphabetical order regardless of charge, and by that rule ammine comes before chlorido, so the two forms beginning with dichlorido are wrongly ordered whatever oxidation state they quote. For the metal: the two ammine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands carry \(-1\) each, so platinum must be \(+2\) for the complex to be neutral. The correct name is diamminedichloridoplatinum(II).

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following is heteroleptic complex ?
rows.solution: A homoleptic complex has all its ligands of one kind; a heteroleptic complex has more than one kind. The hexaamminecobalt, hexaamminechromium and hexaaquanickel ions each carry six identical ligands, so all three are homoleptic. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\) carries four ammine ligands and two chlorido ligands, two different kinds bound to the same metal, so it is the heteroleptic one.

rows.stem: Which of the following molecules is chiral in nature ?
rows.solution: A molecule is chiral if it is not superimposable on its mirror image, and for these compounds that means finding a carbon carrying four different groups. In propan-2-ol the second carbon holds two identical methyl groups, so there is none. In 1-bromobutane the carbon bearing the bromine also holds two hydrogens. In 2-bromopropane the substituted carbon again holds two methyl groups. In butan-2-ol the second carbon carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\), \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(-\mathrm{C_2H_5}\): four different groups, so butan-2-ol is the chiral molecule.

rows.stem: Identify the correct increasing order of boiling points of the given compounds :
rows.solution:
Two effects set the order. Boiling point rises with molecular mass, because the surface available for van der Waals attraction grows; and for the same mass, branching lowers it, because a more compact molecule has less surface in contact with its neighbours.

So propan-1-ol, the lightest, boils first. Of the two butanols, the branched secondary alcohol butan-2-ol boils below the straight-chain butan-1-ol. Pentan-1-ol, the heaviest, boils last. The increasing order is propan-1-ol \(<\) butan-2-ol \(<\) butan-1-ol \(<\) pentan-1-ol.

rows.stem: Identify the compound produced by the reduction of Ethanenitrile with Lithium aluminium hydride :
rows.solution:
Lithium aluminium hydride reduces a nitrile all the way to a primary amine, the triple bond taking up four hydrogen atoms and the carbon skeleton staying intact:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\)
Ethanenitrile has two carbons, so the product has two carbons: ethylamine. Ethanal would be the product of a partial reduction by a milder reagent such as \(\mathrm{DIBAL-H}\), and neither propylamine nor methylamine has the right number of carbons.

rows.stem: The base which is present in DNA but not in RNA is :
rows.solution: DNA and RNA share three bases — adenine, guanine and cytosine — so none of those can distinguish them. The fourth pyrimidine differs: DNA carries thymine, while RNA carries uracil in its place. Thymine is the base present in DNA but not in RNA. The sugar differs too, 2-deoxy-D-ribose in DNA against D-ribose in RNA.

rows.stem: Proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids which are joined to each other by :
rows.solution: Proteins are condensation polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids. The \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) of one residue condenses with the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) of the next, water is eliminated, and the \(-\mathrm{CONH}-\) amide bond that results is called a peptide bond in this context. A glycosidic bond joins sugar units, not amino acids, and while a peptide bond is indeed covalent, naming it merely covalent does not identify it.

rows.stem: Which of the following reactions is not explained by the open chain structure of glucose ?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucose on prolonged heating with HI forms n-hexane.

options.label: B
options.text: Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to form an oxime.

options.label: C
options.text: Glucose gets oxidized to gluconic acid on reaction with bromine water.

options.label: D
options.text: Glucose exists in two different crystalline forms, alpha (\(\alpha\)) and beta (\(\beta\)).

rows.solution:
The open chain aldehyde structure accounts for three of these easily: complete reduction by hydriodic acid to \(n\)-hexane shows a straight six-carbon chain, oxime formation with hydroxylamine shows a carbonyl group, and oxidation by bromine water to gluconic acid shows that carbonyl is an aldehyde.

What it cannot explain is the existence of two crystalline forms, the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) anomers, which differ only in the arrangement at C-1. An open chain has no such centre. This is one of the observations that forced the cyclic hemiacetal structure, in which C-1 becomes a new stereocentre.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The molecularity of the given reaction is 2
\(2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{I_2}\)
Reason (R) : Two molecules of the reactants are involved in simultaneous collision between them.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Molecularity counts the species that must collide at once in an elementary step. The equation shows two molecules of hydrogen iodide coming together, and the decomposition is an elementary bimolecular step, so its molecularity is 2 and the Assertion is true. The Reason states exactly the basis of that count — two reactant molecules taking part in a single simultaneous collision — so it is true as well and it explains the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Zinc, cadmium and mercury are not considered as transition elements.
Reason (R) : These elements have completely filled orbitals in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Zinc, cadmium and mercury have the configuration \((n-1)d^{10}ns^2\), and their common ions \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Hg^{2+}}\) are all \((n-1)d^{10}\). A transition element is defined as one with a partially filled d subshell in its ground state or in one of its common oxidation states, and these three never have one, so they are excluded from the series. Both statements are true, and the second is the definition the first rests on, so the Reason explains the Assertion. The marking scheme for this paper accepts the second code as well, so a student who judged the Reason not to be the explanation is not penalised.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aromatic primary amines can be prepared by Gabriel Phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the anion formed by phthalimide.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis works by having the phthalimide anion displace a halide from an alkyl halide in a nucleophilic substitution. Aryl halides do not undergo that substitution — the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance and the ring repels the incoming nucleophile — so the Reason is true, and it is precisely why the method fails for aromatic amines. Aromatic primary amines therefore cannot be made this way, so the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Glucose gets oxidized to six carbon gluconic acid on reaction with bromine water.
Reason (R) : The carbonyl group is absent in the open chain structure of glucose.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that attacks the aldehyde group alone, so glucose is oxidised to the six-carbon gluconic acid and the Assertion is true. The Reason contradicts it. That oxidation happens precisely because the open chain structure of glucose does contain a carbonyl group, the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) at C-1; saying the carbonyl group is absent is false, and if it were true the reaction could not occur at all. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem: The concentration of the reactant is reduced from 0.6 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) to 0.2 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) in 5 minutes in a first order reaction. Calculate rate constant of the reaction. (log 3 = 0.48)
rows.solution:
For a first order reaction,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Here \([\mathrm{R}]_0 = 0.6\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\), \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.2\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) and \(t = 5\) min, so
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{5}\log\dfrac{0.6}{0.2} = \dfrac{2.303}{5}\log 3 = \dfrac{2.303}{5}\times 0.48\)
\(k = 0.22\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

Note that only the RATIO of the two concentrations enters, which is why a first order rate constant carries units of reciprocal time and nothing else.

rows.stem:
Rate constant k for the first order reaction is \(2.54 \times 10^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Calculate the time required for three-fourth of the reactant to decompose.
(log 4 = 0.60)
rows.solution:
If three-fourths of the reactant has decomposed, one-fourth of it is left, so \([\mathrm{R}] = \tfrac{1}{4}[\mathrm{R}]_0\) and the ratio \([\mathrm{R}]_0/[\mathrm{R}]\) is 4. Rearranging the first order equation for time,
\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{2.303}{2.54 \times 10^{-3}}\log 4\)
\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{2.54 \times 10^{-3}} \times 0.60\)
\(t = 5.44 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{s}\), that is 544 s.

The common slip here is to read "three-fourth decomposed" as "three-fourth remaining" and use \(\log(4/3)\); it is the amount LEFT that goes in the denominator.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) Define activation energy.
(b) Write the unit of rate constant for
(i) zero order reaction, (ii) second order reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that the reactant molecules must possess, over and above their average energy, in order to form the activated complex and cross the energy barrier to products.

(b) The rate constant's units follow from the rate law, since rate always carries units of mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).
(i) For a zero order reaction rate \(= k\), so \(k\) has the units of rate itself: mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).
(ii) For a second order reaction rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^2\), so \(k\) = rate divided by concentration squared: \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\).

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) First ionization enthalpy of Cr is lower than that of Zn. Why ?
(b) Mention any one property of the transition elements which makes them good catalysts.
rows.solution:
(a) Chromium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\) and zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\). Chromium loses a single unpaired \(4s\) electron, and doing so leaves the stable half-filled \(3d^5\) arrangement, so little energy is needed. Zinc must remove an electron from a fully paired \(4s\) orbital, where it feels the repulsion of its partner removed but also the strong pull of a completed \(3d^{10}\) core that shields poorly. The first ionisation enthalpy of chromium is therefore the lower of the two.

(b) Transition elements show variable oxidation states, so they can accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another and thus offer a lower energy route. Any one of several related properties is accepted: vacant d orbitals that let reactants adsorb on the metal surface, the ability to form complexes, or the large surface area of a finely divided metal.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(a) Define coordination number.
(b) Indicate the type of isomerism exhibited by the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The coordination number of a metal ion in a complex is the number of ligand donor atoms to which the metal atom or ion is directly bonded.

(b) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]Cl_3}\) exhibits optical isomerism. Three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands wrap around the cobalt in a propeller arrangement that has no plane of symmetry, so the complex ion exists as two non-superimposable mirror images.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the structure of the given compound :
4-Bromo-3-methylpent-2-ene
(b) What happens when chloroethane is treated with aqueous potassium hydroxide ?
rows.solution:
(a) Number the five-carbon chain so that the double bond gets the lower locant. The double bond lies between C-2 and C-3, a methyl group sits on C-3 and a bromine on C-4:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=C(CH_3)-CHBr-CH_3}\)

(b) Chloroethane heated with aqueous potassium hydroxide undergoes nucleophilic substitution. The hydroxide ion replaces the chlorine and ethanol is formed:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl} + \mathrm{KOH(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{KCl}\)
The medium is what decides the outcome: alcoholic potassium hydroxide would instead eliminate and give ethene.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: When 1.5 g of a non-volatile solute was dissolved in 90 g of benzene, the boiling point of benzene got raised from 353.23 K to 353.93 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (Given \(\mathrm{K_b}\) for benzene = 2.52 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Elevation of boiling point is a colligative property, and for a solution of molality \(m\)
\(\Delta T_b = K_b \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A}\)

The observed elevation is
\(\Delta T_b = 353.93 - 353.23 = 0.70\ \mathrm{K}\)

Substituting \(K_b = 2.52\), \(W_B = 1.5\) g and \(W_A = 90\) g,
\(0.70 = 2.52 \times \dfrac{1.5}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{90}\)
\(M_B = \dfrac{2.52 \times 1.5 \times 1000}{0.70 \times 90} = \dfrac{3780}{63}\)
\(M_B = 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The unit is part of the answer: the marking scheme deducts half a mark if it is missing or wrong.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Sn} \mid \mathrm{Sn^{2+}}\ (0.001\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{H^{+}}\ (0.01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{H_{2(g)}}\ (1\ \mathrm{bar}) \mid \mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Sn^{2+}/Sn}} = -0.14\) V,
\(\mathrm{E^{o}_{H^{+}/H_2}} = 0.00\) V [log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
Tin is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; the hydrogen electrode on the right is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H^+/H_2}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Sn^{2+}/Sn}} = 0 - (-0.14) = 0.14\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Sn(s)} + 2\mathrm{H^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\), so \(n = 2\). With hydrogen at 1 bar its pressure term is 1 and drops out, leaving
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0.14 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.001}{(0.01)^2}\)
\(= 0.14 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log 10\)
\(= 0.14 - 0.0295 = 0.1105\ \mathrm{V}\)

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(a) Complete and balance the following equations :
(i) \(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{513\ \mathrm{K}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow\)
(b) Why is it difficult to separate lanthanoid elements in pure state ?
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Potassium permanganate decomposes on strong heating, the manganese disproportionating into the \(+6\) manganate and the \(+4\) dioxide while oxygen is released:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{513\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

(ii) Sodium dichromate is converted to the potassium salt by adding potassium chloride; potassium dichromate is much the less soluble of the two and crystallises out, which is what drives the exchange:
\(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

(b) The lanthanoids are hard to separate because they are so alike. Lanthanoid contraction makes their ionic radii shrink only very gradually across the series, so neighbouring ions are almost the same size, and since they nearly all occur in the \(+3\) state their chemical and physical properties are very similar too. Separation therefore needs methods that exploit tiny differences, such as ion exchange.

rows.stem:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is diamagnetic whereas \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) is paramagnetic. Justify the statement. [Atomic number of Co = 27]
(b) Write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) on the basis of crystal field theory.
rows.solution:
(a) Cobalt is \(+3\) in both complexes, so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\) in both; the ligands are what differ.

In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) ammonia is a strong field ligand, so the crystal field splitting exceeds the pairing energy. All six d electrons pair up in the lower \(t_{2g}\) set, leaving no unpaired electron, and the complex is diamagnetic.

In \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) the fluoride ion is a weak field ligand, so the splitting is smaller than the pairing energy and the electrons occupy the upper set rather than pair. Four unpaired electrons remain, and the complex is paramagnetic.

(b) When \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) the field is strong, so it costs less to pair electrons in the lower set than to promote one to the upper set. A \(d^4\) ion therefore puts all four electrons into the \(t_{2g}\) orbitals:
\(t_{2g}^4\ e_g^0\)

rows.stem:
(a) Write the major product in the following reactions :
Cyclohexene \(+\ \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\) ?
(b) Define Racemic mixture.
(c) p-dichlorobenzene has a higher melting point as compared to its ortho and meta isomers. Why ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a plain hexagon carrying a single double bond on its right-hand edge, i.e. cyclohexene, followed by '+ Br2 --heat--> ?'. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) With bromine at high temperature the reaction is substitution at the allylic position, not addition across the double bond: the allylic radical formed by removing a hydrogen next to the double bond is resonance stabilised, so that hydrogen is the one replaced. The major product is 3-bromocyclohexene, the ring keeping its double bond with the bromine on the neighbouring carbon.

(b) A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers of a compound, the \(d\) and \(l\) forms. Their rotations are equal and opposite, so they cancel exactly and the mixture is optically inactive.

(c) The para isomer is the most symmetrical of the three, so its molecules pack into the crystal lattice more closely and more regularly than the ortho or meta isomers can. A better packed lattice takes more energy to break down, so p-dichlorobenzene melts at the highest temperature. Note that this argument is about the SOLID state only — it does not carry over to boiling points, which follow dipole moment instead.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the reaction involved in
(a) Rosenmund's reduction
(b) Cannizzaro's reaction
(c) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction
rows.solution:
(a) Rosenmund's reduction. An acyl chloride is hydrogenated over palladium supported on barium sulphate, a catalyst deliberately poisoned so that the reduction stops at the aldehyde instead of going on to the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

(b) Cannizzaro's reaction. An aldehyde with no \(\alpha\) hydrogen, treated with concentrated alkali, disproportionates: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidised to the salt of the acid:
\(2\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{KOH\ (conc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOOK}\)

(c) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction. A carboxylic acid bearing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen is halogenated at that position by chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus, and hydrolysis gives the \(\alpha\)-halo acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{CH_3CHClCOOH}\)

rows.stem:
Define the following term :
(a) Reducing sugar
(b) Differentiate between the following :
(i) Fibrous proteins and globular proteins
(ii) Nucleotide and nucleoside
rows.solution:
(a) A reducing sugar is a carbohydrate that reduces Fehling's solution or Tollens' reagent. All monosaccharides do so, and those disaccharides in which a free aldehydic or ketonic group remains, such as maltose and lactose.

(b)(i) In a fibrous protein the polypeptide chains run parallel to one another and are held together by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a thread-like structure that is insoluble in water; keratin and myosin are examples. In a globular protein the chain coils around on itself into a roughly spherical shape, and these are usually soluble in water; insulin and albumin are examples.

(ii) A nucleoside is the unit formed when a nitrogenous base is attached to a sugar, so nucleoside = base + sugar. A nucleotide is what results when that nucleoside is further linked to phosphoric acid, so nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate. It is the nucleotide, not the nucleoside, that is the repeating unit of a nucleic acid.

rows.stem:
Write the reaction of glucose with the following :
(a) \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\)
(c) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Hydroxylamine attacks the free aldehyde group at C-1 and water is eliminated, giving glucose oxime. This reaction is evidence for the carbonyl group in the open chain form:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N-OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH{=}N-OH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

(b) Acetic anhydride acetylates every hydroxyl group. Glucose has five of them, four secondary and one primary, so the product is glucose pentaacetate — the reaction that establishes how many \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups the molecule carries:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)

(c) Concentrated nitric acid is a strong enough oxidant to attack both ends of the chain, turning the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) and the terminal \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) into \(-\mathrm{COOH}\). The product is the dicarboxylic saccharic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Calculate the amount of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) (i = 2.59) dissolved in 2.46 litre of water such that its osmotic pressure is 0.70 atm at 27°C.
[Given : R = 0.082 L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), molar mass of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) = 111 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.context: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood's osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar.
rows.solution:
Calcium chloride dissociates, so the van't Hoff factor enters the osmotic pressure equation:
\(\Pi = i\,C\,RT = i \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1}{V} \times RT\)

Substituting \(\Pi = 0.70\) atm, \(i = 2.59\), \(M_B = 111\) g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(V = 2.46\) L, \(R = 0.082\) L atm \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(T = 27 + 273 = 300\) K:
\(0.70 = 2.59 \times \dfrac{W_B}{111} \times \dfrac{1}{2.46} \times 0.082 \times 300\)

Rearranging,
\(W_B = \dfrac{0.70 \times 111 \times 2.46}{2.59 \times 0.082 \times 300}\)
\(W_B = 3\ \mathrm{g}\)

The temperature must be converted to kelvin before it is used; leaving it at 27 would change the answer by a factor of eleven.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: When raisins are kept in water, they get swollen. Name the phenomenon involved in this process.
rows.context: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood's osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar.
rows.solution: Osmosis. The water outside the raisin is the region of lower solute concentration and the sugary interior the region of higher concentration, so water passes inward through the raisin's skin, which acts as a semi-permeable membrane, and the raisin swells.

rows.stem: Why osmotic pressure is more advantageous than other colligative properties ?
rows.context: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood's osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar.
rows.solution: Osmotic pressure has the practical advantage that its magnitude is large even for a very dilute solution, so it can be measured accurately where a freezing point depression or boiling point elevation would be too small to read reliably. It is also measured at room temperature rather than at a boiling or freezing point, which matters for substances such as proteins that would be destroyed by heating, and it uses molarity, which is measured directly by volume.

rows.stem: Which phenomenon is responsible for desalination of sea water ?

Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. rows.solution: Reverse osmosis. Applying to the sea water a pressure greater than its osmotic pressure drives the solvent backwards through the semi-permeable membrane, from the concentrated side to the pure side, so fresh water is collected and the salts are left behind.

rows.stem:
Complete the following equations :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)\ LiAlH_4}}\)
(ii) 4-nitrotoluene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe + HCl}}\)
rows.context: Like \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order \(1^{\mathrm{o}} > 2^{\mathrm{o}} > 3^{\mathrm{o}}\). It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (ii)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a benzene ring carrying NO2 at the top and CH3 at the para position, with 'Fe + HCl' over the arrow. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) Lithium aluminium hydride reduces the amide right down to the amine, removing the carbonyl oxygen and keeping both carbons, so ethanamide gives ethylamine:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\)

(ii) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces an aromatic nitro group to a primary amino group, leaving the ring and the methyl group untouched, so 4-nitrotoluene gives 4-methylaniline:
\(\mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{4\text{-}H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3}\)
Iron and hydrochloric acid are preferred to tin and hydrochloric acid because the \(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\) formed is hydrolysed in the reaction mixture, so the acid is regenerated and only a small amount is needed.

rows.stem: Why primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines ?
rows.context: Like \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order \(1^{\mathrm{o}} > 2^{\mathrm{o}} > 3^{\mathrm{o}}\). It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc.
rows.solution: A primary amine has two hydrogen atoms on nitrogen, so its molecules associate with one another through intermolecular hydrogen bonds, and energy must be supplied to break that network before the liquid can boil. A tertiary amine has all three valencies of nitrogen taken by alkyl groups and no hydrogen left on nitrogen at all, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. With only weaker van der Waals forces to overcome, tertiary amines boil at lower temperatures.

rows.stem:
Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_{10}H_7 - N(CH_3)_2}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C_{10}H_7 - NH_2}\)
(the \(\mathrm{C_{10}H_7}\) group is naphthalen-2-yl in both)
rows.context: Like \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order \(1^{\mathrm{o}} > 2^{\mathrm{o}} > 3^{\mathrm{o}}\). It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — both sub-parts are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS: a fused two-ring naphthalene carrying, at the 2 (beta) position, N(CH3)2 in (i) and NH2 in (ii). Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) The nitrogen carries two methyl groups and the naphthalenyl group, so all three of its valencies are taken by carbon: this is a tertiary amine.
(ii) The nitrogen carries the naphthalenyl group and two hydrogens, so only one of its valencies is taken by carbon: this is a primary amine.

rows.stem: Out of Butan-1-amine and Butan-1-ol, which is more soluble in water ?
rows.context: Like \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order \(1^{\mathrm{o}} > 2^{\mathrm{o}} > 3^{\mathrm{o}}\). It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc.
rows.solution: Butan-1-ol is the more soluble in water. Both molecules can form hydrogen bonds with water, but oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond of the alcohol is the more polarised and the hydrogen bonds it makes with water are the stronger. With hydrocarbon chains of the same length on each, that difference decides it.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) How will you convert the following :
(i) Propanone to Propene
(ii) Benzoic acid to Benzaldehyde
(iii) Benzene to m-Nitroacetophenone
(b) (i) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN :
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=O}\), \(\mathrm{((CH_3)_3C)_2C=O}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH=O}\)
(ii) Identify the compounds, which would undergo Aldol condensation :
HCHO, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), cyclohexanone
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (b)(i)'s three carbonyl compounds are printed as 2-D structural drawings (two substituents bracketed onto each C=O), and (b)(ii)'s fourth compound is a skeletal hexagon carrying a doubly-bonded O, i.e. cyclohexanone. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Propanone to propene, in two steps. Lithium aluminium hydride reduces the ketone to the secondary alcohol, and concentrated sulphuric acid then dehydrates it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2}\)

(ii) Benzoic acid to benzaldehyde. The acid is first converted to its acyl chloride with thionyl chloride, and Rosenmund's reduction over poisoned palladium then stops at the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}]{\mathrm{H_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

(iii) Benzene to m-nitroacetophenone. The ORDER of the two steps is the whole question. Acylate first: Friedel-Crafts acylation gives acetophenone, and the \(-\mathrm{COCH_3}\) group is deactivating and meta directing, so the nitration that follows delivers the nitro group to the meta position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{\mathrm{CH_3COCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{3\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}COCH_3}\)
Nitrating first would give nitrobenzene, which is too deactivated to acylate at all.

(b)(i) Addition of \(\mathrm{HCN}\) gets harder as the carbonyl carbon is made less electrophilic by electron-donating alkyl groups and more shielded by their bulk. Two tert-butyl groups do both to an extreme degree, two methyl groups do it moderately, and one methyl with one hydrogen least of all. The increasing order of reactivity is
\(((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C})_2\mathrm{C{=}O} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}O} < \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}O}\)

(ii) Aldol condensation needs at least one \(\alpha\) hydrogen, a hydrogen on the carbon next to the carbonyl. Methanal has no carbon next to its carbonyl at all, and in benzaldehyde that neighbour is part of the ring and carries no hydrogen, so neither reacts. Ethanal has a methyl group and cyclohexanone has \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups on both sides of its carbonyl, so those two undergo aldol condensation.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) Give chemical tests to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds :
(i) Acetophenone and Benzophenone
(ii) Propanal and Propanone
(iii) Pentan-2-one and Pentan-3-one
(b) (i) Which of the following acids is stronger and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_2FCOOH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)
(ii) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their boiling points :
\(\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Acetophenone and benzophenone: use the iodoform test. Acetophenone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group, so warming it with sodium hydroxide and iodine gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; benzophenone has phenyl groups on both sides of the carbonyl and gives none.

(ii) Propanal and propanone: use Tollens' reagent. Propanal is an aldehyde and reduces it, depositing a silver mirror; propanone is a ketone and does not.

(iii) Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one: use the iodoform test again. Pentan-2-one has its carbonyl next to a methyl group and gives the yellow precipitate; in pentan-3-one the carbonyl sits between two ethyl groups, so it does not.

(b)(i) \(\mathrm{CH_2FCOOH}\) is the stronger acid. Fluorine is strongly electronegative and withdraws electron density along the chain by the \(-I\) effect, which spreads and stabilises the negative charge of the carboxylate ion left behind when the proton leaves. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid. The methyl group of acetic acid does the opposite, pushing electron density towards the carboxylate and destabilising it.

(ii) Boiling point rises with the strength of the intermolecular forces. Propane is non-polar and has only weak van der Waals forces. Dimethyl ether is polar but its oxygen carries no hydrogen, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. Ethanal is more polar still, with a strong carbonyl dipole. Ethanol has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group and its molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which costs the most energy to break. The increasing order is
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3OCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)

rows.stem:
(a) The conductivity of 0.1 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) solution of NaCl is \(1.06 \times 10^{-2}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation.
\(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na^{+}}} = 50.1\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^{-}}} = 76.5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)
(b) (i) Following cell reaction occurs in a galvanic cell :
\(2\mathrm{Ag^{+}_{(aq)}} + \mathrm{Zn_{(s)}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag_{(s)}} + \mathrm{Zn^{2+}_{(aq)}}\) \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{(cell)}} = +1.56\) V
Predict the direction of flow of current.
(ii) Differentiate between a primary battery and a secondary battery.
rows.solution:
(a) The limiting molar conductivity comes from Kohlrausch's law, adding the two ionic contributions:
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NaCl}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na^+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}} = 50.1 + 76.5 = 126.6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The molar conductivity at this concentration follows from the conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M} = \dfrac{1.06 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000}{0.1} = 106\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

and the degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{106}{126.6} = 0.8372\), that is \(83.72\%\).

(b)(i) Zinc is oxidised and silver ions reduced, so electrons leave the zinc, travel through the external wire and arrive at the silver. Conventional current flows the opposite way to the electrons: from silver to zinc in the external circuit, that is from cathode to anode.

(ii) A primary battery's reaction happens once and cannot be reversed, so the cell is discarded when the reactants are used up — a dry cell or a mercury cell. A secondary battery's reaction can be reversed by passing current back through it, so it can be recharged and used repeatedly — a lead storage battery or a nickel-cadmium cell.

rows.stem:
(a) Resistance of a conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl solution is 100 \(\Omega\). If the resistance of the same cell when filled with 0.01 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) KCl solution is 300 \(\Omega\), calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of 0.01 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) KCl solution. The conductivity of 0.1 M KCl solution is \(1.29 \times 10^{-2}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).
(b) (i) Write any two advantages of \(\mathrm{H_2 - O_2}\) fuel cell.
(ii) Why does the cell potential of mercury cell remain constant throughout the life ?
rows.solution:
(a) Both measurements use the same cell, so the cell constant found from the first solution applies to the second.
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{R}\left(\dfrac{l}{A}\right) \implies \dfrac{l}{A} = \kappa R\)
\(\dfrac{l}{A} = 1.29 \times 10^{-2} \times 100 = 1.29\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

For the 0.01 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) solution, whose resistance is \(300\ \Omega\),
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{300} \times 1.29 = 0.0043\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

and
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M} = \dfrac{0.0043 \times 1000}{0.01} = 430\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

(b)(i) A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is pollution free, its only product being water, and it is highly efficient, since it converts chemical energy to electrical energy directly rather than through heat. It also runs continuously as long as the gases are supplied.

(ii) The overall reaction of a mercury cell is \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\), in which every species is a solid or a liquid. No ion in solution appears in the reaction quotient, so nothing in the Nernst expression changes as the cell discharges and the potential stays constant throughout its life.

rows.stem: An organic compound 'A', with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\) reacts with active metals such as sodium to give compound 'B' and hydrogen gas. 'A' on treatment with iodine and sodium hydroxide gives 'C' and in presence of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 413 K gives 'D' (\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\)). 'D' on reaction with excess of HI gives 'E'. Identify 'A', 'B', 'C', 'D' and 'E' and write all the reactions involved.
rows.solution:
The formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\) with the reactions given identifies 'A' as ethanol, and everything else follows from it.

'A' releases hydrogen with sodium, which is the reaction of an alcoholic \(-\mathrm{OH}\), giving the alkoxide:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + 2\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2ONa} + \mathrm{H_2}\)
so \(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2ONa}\), sodium ethoxide.

Iodine with sodium hydroxide gives the iodoform test, which ethanol answers because it has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)}-\) group:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{NaOH}]{\mathrm{I_2},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CHI_3} + \mathrm{HCOONa}\)
so \(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform.

Sulphuric acid at 413 K is the lower of the two dehydration temperatures and gives the ether rather than the alkene, which matches the formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) quoted in the question:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
so \(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3}\), ethoxyethane.

Excess hydroiodic acid cleaves the ether at both \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bonds:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3} + 2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
so \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2I}\), iodoethane.

So 'A' is ethanol, 'B' sodium ethoxide, 'C' iodoform, 'D' ethoxyethane and 'E' iodoethane.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the reagents which are used in the given conversions :
(i) Phenol to 2, 4, 6 - tribromophenol
(ii) Propene to propan-1-ol
(iii) Butan-2-one to butan-2-ol
(b) Explain the mechanism of acid catalyzed hydration of alkene to form corresponding alcohol.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Phenol to 2,4,6-tribromophenol: bromine water. The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group activates the ring so strongly that all three available positions are brominated at once and a white precipitate separates.
(ii) Propene to propan-1-ol: this is anti-Markovnikov addition, since the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) must end up on the terminal carbon. Use hydrogen bromide in the presence of a peroxide followed by hydrolysis, or diborane followed by hydrogen peroxide in alkali.
(iii) Butan-2-one to butan-2-ol: any reducing agent for a ketone will do — hydrogen over nickel, palladium or platinum, or lithium aluminium hydride, or sodium borohydride.

(b) Acid catalysed hydration of an alkene adds water across the double bond in three steps, and the Markovnikov orientation comes out of the middle one.

Step 1 — protonation of the alkene. The \(\pi\) electrons attack a proton from the hydronium ion, giving a carbocation. Of the two possible cations the more substituted one forms, because it is the more stable, and that is what puts the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) on the more substituted carbon at the end.

Step 2 — nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation. A water molecule donates a lone pair to the positively charged carbon, giving a protonated alcohol, an oxonium ion.

Step 3 — deprotonation. Another water molecule removes the extra proton from the oxonium ion, giving the alcohol and regenerating the hydronium ion. The catalyst is returned unchanged, which is what makes it a catalyst.
